title: Nandabala's milk
hook: after the fasting, a herdsman's daughter gives him milk-rice (Buddhacarita 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothingness, and your line: not final. Did you finish something and ask what came next? Today the search goes as far as a body can go. Day seven hundred fourteen.

A bowl of rice cooked in milk. Plain food, the kind a grandmother makes for someone who's been sick. In this canto it changes the story. The prince has left his teachers. He's gone to live by a river, and now, with no one left to learn from, he tries the one road he hasn't tried: fasting, as hard as a body can bear. In the penance grove he told the ascetics that pain wasn't the way. Now he tests it on himself.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK-RICE.` → `NO TEACHERS LEFT.` → `HE TESTS THE HARD ROAD HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the fasting. On the bank of the river Nairanjana, the poem says, he cuts his food down and down, until he lives on almost nothing. His body wastes away. Some companions, also seeking freedom, settle near him, admiring his discipline and waiting for him to break through. Second, the turn. He doesn't break through. He breaks down. And in the poem, paraphrased here, he sees why: this isn't the way to freedom. A mind can't settle when the body is starving. Calm needs some strength under it. Third, the milk. He bathes in the river, weak, and comes up out of the water slowly. And then comes Nandabala, the daughter of a chief of the herdsmen, moved by the gods, the poem says, to come to him. She bows and offers him a bowl of milk-rice. He takes it. He eats. And strength returns. Fourth, the cost. His companions watch him eat and decide he has given up. They leave him. The poem doesn't defend him to them. It just lets the moment be. A woman with a bowl did what no teacher and no hardship could: she gave him back his body, so his mind could do its work. Other tellings give the woman a different name, Sujata, and tell the scene with other details. This poem calls her Nandabala. Either way, a herdsman's daughter stands where the great teachers stood. And here's this whole week, looking back. A grove that sought heaven through pain. A palace in grief. Ministers with every argument. A king with half a kingdom. Fire that fuel can't quench. A teacher whose best was not final. And now a bowl of milk-rice, taken with thanks. The search has passed through every door that was offered. What's left is a tree, and the night.
screen: `FASTING BY THE RIVER.` · `A STARVED BODY, AN UNSETTLED MIND.` · `NANDABALA'S BOWL.` · `HIS COMPANIONS WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `STRENGTH RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept help today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where you've been going it alone, harder than you need to. A task. A worry. A long week. Now bring to mind one person who has offered help, or would if you asked. Picture them holding out a bowl. Notice what in you wants to wave it away. Then, just for the sit, picture taking it, with both hands, and saying thank you. Feel what changes in your body when you're not carrying it alone. The bell holds the time.
Nandabala's milk. After fasting brings him no closer, a herdsman's daughter offers the prince milk-rice; he eats, his strength returns, and his companions leave him. Today's word.
Your line: strength returns. Today, accept one offer of help, a meal, a ride, a hand with something heavy, and let it actually help. Day seven hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: The offering of milk-rice is remembered in Buddhist art and festivals, and giving food to monks and nuns is a daily practice in some Buddhist communities, where the gift is received as part of the path.

what a scholar hears: this poem names the giver Nandabala, while other tellings call her Sujata; the scene marks the turn from self-mortification toward a middle path.
